awd_titl_txt: CAREER: Soft, biocompatible ion-based transistors for responsive neuroelectronic devices
awd_abstract_narration:
Bioelectronic devices have numerous potential benefits to human health, from in-home wellness monitoring to diagnosis and treatment of neuropsychiatric diseases. However, safe and effective use of these devices is limited by the rigid, non-biocompatible electronic components that must be incorporated to allow execution of the required functions. This project seeks to study how soft and fully biocompatible materials can be leveraged to interact directly with signals from the body without damaging tissue. A transistor fabricated from these materials will be used to create the circuits necessary for bioelectronic devices to acquire and modulate the activity of neurons in the brain. The outcome of the research will benefit society by improving the design of bioelectronic devices currently used for patients with conditions such as epilepsy or Parkinson's disease by eliminating the need for implantation of bulky or rigid materials in the body. This project will also facilitate understanding of the principles underlying interactions between the body and electronic devices. The educational component of this project leverages ion-gated transistors as biocompatible and low-cost components to be used in student and educator projects that teach principles of bioelectronic device design. These projects will be maintained in a comprehensive database to facilitate dissemination to educators and outreach coordinators, providing evidence-based methods to improve project-based learning in bioelectronics more broadly. The educational objectives of the project are to provide students and educators with hands-on opportunities to design and test simple, biocompatible bioelectronic devices. These efforts will increase exposure to engineering methods in schools and stimulate interest in bioelectronics to benefit health.

There is an enormous need to develop bioelectronic components that can merge biocompatibility, ion transduction, high speed, and reliable operation in physiological environments. The objective of the project is to develop ion-driven, conformable, implantable bioelectronic devices to enable efficient interaction with neural circuits. The central hypothesis is that ion-gated transistors will effectively interact with neural signals because they can directly transduce the brain's ionic flux, and are sufficient to create the integrated circuits required for fully implantable, soft, closed-loop devices that do not require rigid encapsulation. The research involves fabrication of integrated circuits comprised of ion-gated transistors with comprehensive in vitro and modeling-based characterization of the parameters governing their operation in physiologic environments. These devices are then used to modulate neural networks in an in vivo animal model of epilepsy and acquire neurophysiologic data from human subjects. The rationale underlying this research is that realization of such devices will transform design of bioelectronic devices with the potential to enhance diagnosis and therapy for neuropsychiatric disease.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project set out to develop a new kind of electronic device that can communicate with brain circuits in their own language. Ordinary electronics work by moving electrons through metal and silicon. Living tissue works differently: it sends signals by moving ions through salty fluid. Bridging those two worlds has long required bulky, rigid packaging that protects the electronics from the body but makes implants stiff, expensive, and risky. Our goal was to remove that barrier by developing the internal ion-gated transistor, or IGT, a soft component that responds directly to the ionic signals of the nervous system.

All of the work we proposed was completed, and the results confirmed our central idea. We first showed that IGTs can serve as the building blocks of complete circuits, not just single sensors. Using them, we built amplifiers and logic elements small enough to sit directly on tissue while still operating fast enough to keep up with real brain activity. We tested how long these circuits survive in conditions that mimic the body. They remained stable over extended periods without the hard encapsulation that conventional implants depend on, which was the key practical question standing in the way of soft implantable electronics.

With reliable circuits in hand, we moved to a living system. In an animal model of epilepsy, IGT-based devices recorded neural activity and delivered stimulation in response to what they detected, forming a closed loop that ran for long stretches without failing. Finally, we confirmed that the same devices can be scaled and fabricated for use with human subjects, an essential step toward eventual clinical use.

The broader significance is twofold. Scientifically, IGTs give researchers a way to record from and stimulate many points in a neural circuit at once, at a level of detail that was not previously achievable. That opens up questions about neural network function that simply could not be tested before. Medically, the devices point toward implants that are thinner, softer, simpler to manufacture, and less likely to injure delicate tissue. Because the materials involved are inexpensive and biocompatible, the same approach extends beyond the operating room to everyday health technology: comfortable sleep monitors, skin-mounted heart-rate patches, seizure alerting, and fall prevention. We have shared our devices and methods with engineers in both academic and commercial settings so that these benefits can reach real products.

The project also invested in society. A new hands-on undergraduate and graduate course on nanoscience and microfabrication gave students the chance to design, build, and test their own bioelectronic devices in a working cleanroom. Junior high and high school students from a range of socioeconomic backgrounds spent summers in the laboratory, several of them building working prototypes including a wearable EEG headband that detects the onset of sleep and an adhesive heart-rate sensor. A summer professional development position brought science teachers into the lab, where they gained practical experience, helped mentor the student researchers, and left with concrete laboratory projects to bring back to their own classrooms. Taken together, the project delivered a working technology, a clearer understanding of how electronics and living tissue can be joined, and a pipeline of students and teachers equipped to carry that work forward.
